claim: Development and aging of the cerebral cortex show similar topographic organization.
source: Development and aging of the cerebral cortex show similar topographic organization and are governed by the same genes.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known fact that sets up the research question about subcortical regions.

claim: Development and aging of the cerebral cortex are governed by the same genes.
source: Development and aging of the cerebral cortex show similar topographic organization and are governed by the same genes.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as established knowledge.

claim: It is unclear whether the same is true for subcortical regions.
source: It is unclear whether the same is true for subcortical regions, which follow fundamentally different ontogenetic and phylogenetic principles.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in knowledge that motivates the study.

claim: Subcortical regions follow fundamentally different ontogenetic and phylogenetic principles than the cerebral cortex.
source: It is unclear whether the same is true for subcortical regions, which follow fundamentally different ontogenetic and phylogenetic principles.
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge in the abstract.

claim: The study analyzed over 6000 longitudinal MRIs of the brain.
source: Analyzing over 6000 longitudinal MRIs of the brain, we used graph theory to identify five clusters of coordinated development, indexed as patterns of correlated volumetric change in brain structures.
evidence: This describes the dataset used in the study.

claim: Graph theory was used to identify five clusters of coordinated development.
source: Analyzing over 6000 longitudinal MRIs of the brain, we used graph theory to identify five clusters of coordinated development, indexed as patterns of correlated volumetric change in brain structures.
evidence: This describes the analytical method and main finding.

claim: Coordinated development was indexed as patterns of correlated volumetric change in brain structures.
source: Analyzing over 6000 longitudinal MRIs of the brain, we used graph theory to identify five clusters of coordinated development, indexed as patterns of correlated volumetric change in brain structures.
evidence: This describes the operational definition used in the study.

claim: The clusters tended to follow placement along the cranial axis in embryonic brain development.
source: The clusters tended to follow placement along the cranial axis in embryonic brain development, suggesting continuity from prenatal stages, and correlated with cognition.
evidence: This is a main finding of the study based on comparison with embryonic developmental principles.

claim: The clustering pattern suggests continuity from prenatal stages.
source: The clusters tended to follow placement along the cranial axis in embryonic brain development, suggesting continuity from prenatal stages, and correlated with cognition.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the finding about cranial axis organization.

claim: The clusters correlated with cognition.
source: The clusters tended to follow placement along the cranial axis in embryonic brain development, suggesting continuity from prenatal stages, and correlated with cognition.
evidence: This is stated as a finding in the abstract.

claim: Developmental clusters were conserved through life across independent longitudinal datasets.
source: Across independent longitudinal datasets, we demonstrated that developmental clusters were conserved through life.
evidence: This is a main finding based on analysis of multiple datasets.

claim: Twin-based genetic correlations revealed distinct sets of genes governing change in each cluster.
source: Twin-based genetic correlations revealed distinct sets of genes governing change in each cluster.
evidence: This is a finding from the twin study analysis.

claim: Single-nucleotide polymorphisms-based analyses of 38,127 cross-sectional MRIs showed a similar pattern of genetic volume–volume correlations.
source: Single-nucleotide polymorphisms-based analyses of 38,127 cross-sectional MRIs showed a similar pattern of genetic volume–volume correlations.
evidence: This describes a finding from the SNP-based genetic analysis.

claim: Coordination of subcortical change adheres to fundamental principles of lifespan continuity and genetic organization.
source: In conclusion, coordination of subcortical change adheres to fundamental principles of lifespan continuity and genetic organization.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study based on all findings.

claim: Cortical development follows a topographic organization through childhood and adolescence.
source: Cortical development follows a topographic organization through childhood and adolescence (Fjell et al., 2019; Krongold et al., 2017; Raznahan et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Regions of the cortex with similar structural and functional properties tend to develop together.
source: This means that regions of the cortex with similar structural and functional properties tend to develop together (see Eickhoff et al., 2018 for a discussion of cortical topography in the context of neuroimaging).
evidence: This is supported by a citation and explains the concept of topographic organization.

claim: Cortical topography is conserved through later development and aging.
source: This topography is conserved through later development and aging (Fjell et al., 2019; Tamnes et al., 2013) and follows the genetic organization of the cortex, i.e. is controlled by overlapping sets of genes (Fjell et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Cortical topography follows the genetic organization of the cortex and is controlled by overlapping sets of genes.
source: This topography is conserved through later development and aging (Fjell et al., 2019; Tamnes et al., 2013) and follows the genetic organization of the cortex, i.e. is controlled by overlapping sets of genes (Fjell et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: It is not known whether the same is true for subcortical structures.
source: It is not known whether the same is true for subcortical structures.
evidence: This identifies a knowledge gap that motivates the study.

claim: The cerebral cortex shows monotone thinning across the lifespan.
source: In contrast to the monotone thinning of the cerebral cortex (Storsve et al., 2014), lifespan trajectories of subcortical structures are more diverse and complex (Allen et al., 2005; Narvacan et al., 2017; Raznahan et al., 2014; Walhovd et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Lifespan trajectories of subcortical structures are more diverse and complex than those of the cerebral cortex.
source: In contrast to the monotone thinning of the cerebral cortex (Storsve et al., 2014), lifespan trajectories of subcortical structures are more diverse and complex (Allen et al., 2005; Narvacan et al., 2017; Raznahan et al., 2014; Walhovd et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The diverse and complex trajectories of subcortical structures may be due to fundamental ontogenetic and phylogenetic differences between cortical and subcortical regions.
source: This may be due to fundamental ontogenetic and phylogenetic differences between cortical and subcortical regions.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for observed differences.

claim: The embryonic origin of the cortex is the pallium.
source: The embryonic origin of the cortex is the pallium, while cerebellar and subcortical structures originate from the hindbrain, diencephalon, or subpallium (Tuller et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Cerebellar and subcortical structures originate from the hindbrain, diencephalon, or subpallium.
source: The embryonic origin of the cortex is the pallium, while cerebellar and subcortical structures originate from the hindbrain, diencephalon, or subpallium (Tuller et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Subcortical structures can be placed according to their position along the cranial vertical axis.
source: These structures can be placed according to their position along the cranial vertical axis (see Table 2).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Table 2.

claim: The subcortex is evolutionary older than the cortex.
source: Although the subcortex is evolutionary older than the cortex, it has a higher proportion of evolutionarily more recent genes, and a higher evolutionary rate, which is a basic measure of evolution at the molecular level (Tuller et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The subcortex has a higher proportion of evolutionarily more recent genes than the cortex.
source: Although the subcortex is evolutionary older than the cortex, it has a higher proportion of evolutionarily more recent genes, and a higher evolutionary rate, which is a basic measure of evolution at the molecular level (Tuller et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The subcortex has a higher evolutionary rate than the cortex.
source: Although the subcortex is evolutionary older than the cortex, it has a higher proportion of evolutionarily more recent genes, and a higher evolutionary rate, which is a basic measure of evolution at the molecular level (Tuller et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Genes expressed in the subcortex generally are more region specific.
source: It has also been argued that genes expressed in the subcortex generally are more region specific (Tuller et al., 2008; Zhang and Li, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Phylogenetically older structures show higher plasticity and potential for change in response to environmental impacts in human development and aging.
source: These mechanisms may be seen in human development and aging, with higher plasticity and potential for change in response to environmental impacts in phylogenetically older structures (Walhovd et al., 2016b), especially the hippocampus (Engvig et al., 2014; Eriksson et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The hippocampus shows especially high plasticity and potential for change in response to environmental impacts.
source: These mechanisms may be seen in human development and aging, with higher plasticity and potential for change in response to environmental impacts in phylogenetically older structures (Walhovd et al., 2016b), especially the hippocampus (Engvig et al., 2014; Eriksson et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The combination of plasticity and vulnerability could contribute to the larger diversity in the lifespan trajectories of subcortical structures.
source: This combination of plasticity and vulnerability could contribute to the larger diversity in the lifespan trajectories of subcortical structures (Walhovd et al., 2005).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation supported by a citation.

claim: A hypothesis is that genetically governed neurodevelopmental processes can be traced in the brain later in life.
source: On the other hand, a hypothesis is that genetically governed neurodevelopmental processes can be traced in the brain later in life (Chen et al., 2011; Satizabal et al., 2019).
evidence: This hypothesis is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Brain regions under shared genetic control in development continue to be influenced by the same genes and change together through life.
source: This would for instance entail that brain regions under shared genetic control in development continue to be influenced by the same genes and change together through life.
evidence: This is a logical consequence of the hypothesis stated.

claim: Shared genetic control of cortical regions in development continuing through life has been shown for the comparably less plastic cortex.
source: This has been shown for the comparably less plastic cortex (Fjell et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: It is not known whether patterns of subcortical maturation in childhood can be traced back to principles of embryonic development.
source: In light of the diverse age trajectories and high plasticity of subcortical structures, it is not known whether patterns of subcortical maturation in childhood can be traced back to principles of embryonic development, how developmental organization sets constraints on subcortical aging, and the degree to which this organization of change is under common genetic control.
evidence: This identifies a knowledge gap that the study addresses.

claim: It is not known how developmental organization sets constraints on subcortical aging.
source: In light of the diverse age trajectories and high plasticity of subcortical structures, it is not known whether patterns of subcortical maturation in childhood can be traced back to principles of embryonic development, how developmental organization sets constraints on subcortical aging, and the degree to which this organization of change is under common genetic control.
evidence: This identifies a knowledge gap that the study addresses.

claim: It is not known the degree to which the organization of subcortical change is under common genetic control.
source: In light of the diverse age trajectories and high plasticity of subcortical structures, it is not known whether patterns of subcortical maturation in childhood can be traced back to principles of embryonic development, how developmental organization sets constraints on subcortical aging, and the degree to which this organization of change is under common genetic control.
evidence: This identifies a knowledge gap that the study addresses.

claim: The study tested how subcortical developmental volumetric change clustered across different structures.
source: Specifically, we tested how subcortical developmental volumetric change clustered across different structures, how similar this organization was in development versus aging, and whether clusters of change were influenced by shared genetics.
evidence: This describes one of the main research questions.

claim: The study tested how similar the organization of subcortical change was in development versus aging.
source: Specifically, we tested how subcortical developmental volumetric change clustered across different structures, how similar this organization was in development versus aging, and whether clusters of change were influenced by shared genetics.
evidence: This describes one of the main research questions.

claim: The study tested whether clusters of subcortical change were influenced by shared genetics.
source: Specifically, we tested how subcortical developmental volumetric change clustered across different structures, how similar this organization was in development versus aging, and whether clusters of change were influenced by shared genetics.
evidence: This describes one of the main research questions.

claim: The study hypothesized that volumetric changes in the developmental structures would tend to cluster according to embryonic principles, i.e. placement along the cranial vertical axis.
source: We hypothesized that volumetric changes in the developmental structures would tend to cluster according to embryonic principles, i.e. placement along the cranial vertical axis, that the pattern of change in aging would be similar to the pattern of change detected in childhood, and that structures changing together throughout the life would be governed by the same sets of genes.
evidence: This is an explicit statement of one of the study's hypotheses.

claim: The study hypothesized that the pattern of change in aging would be similar to the pattern of change detected in childhood.
source: We hypothesized that volumetric changes in the developmental structures would tend to cluster according to embryonic principles, i.e. placement along the cranial vertical axis, that the pattern of change in aging would be similar to the pattern of change detected in childhood, and that structures changing together throughout the life would be governed by the same sets of genes.
evidence: This is an explicit statement of one of the study's hypotheses.

claim: The study hypothesized that structures changing together throughout the life would be governed by the same sets of genes.
source: We hypothesized that volumetric changes in the developmental structures would tend to cluster according to embryonic principles, i.e. placement along the cranial vertical axis, that the pattern of change in aging would be similar to the pattern of change detected in childhood, and that structures changing together throughout the life would be governed by the same sets of genes.
evidence: This is an explicit statement of one of the study's hypotheses.

claim: The LCBC dataset comprised 974 healthy participants from 4.1 to 88.5 years with a total of 1633 MRI examinations.
source: A single-center longitudinal dataset (Center for Lifespan Changes in Brain and Cognition [LCBC]), comprising 974 healthy participants from 4.1 to 88.5 years with a total of 1633 MRI examinations, was used.
evidence: This describes the dataset used for the initial analysis.

claim: The LCBC sample was divided into development (<20 years, n = 644, 1021 MRIs) and adulthood/aging (≥20 years, n = 330, 612 MRIs).
source: The sample was divided into development and adulthood/aging (development [<20 years], n = 644, 1021 MRIs, follow-up interval = 1.7 years [1.0–3.2]; adulthood/aging [≥20 years], n = 330, 612 MRIs, follow-up interval = 1.6 years [0.2–6.6]), see Fjell et al., 2015 for details (sample descriptives are provided in Table 1).
evidence: This describes how the sample was divided for analysis.

claim: The mean follow-up interval for the development group was 1.7 years (1.0–3.2).
source: The sample was divided into development and adulthood/aging (development [<20 years], n = 644, 1021 MRIs, follow-up interval = 1.7 years [1.0–3.2]; adulthood/aging [≥20 years], n = 330, 612 MRIs, follow-up interval = 1.6 years [0.2–6.6]), see Fjell et al., 2015 for details (sample descriptives are provided in Table 1).
evidence: This is a descriptive statistic of the dataset.

claim: The mean follow-up interval for the adulthood/aging group was 1.6 years (0.2–6.6).
source: The sample was divided into development and adulthood/aging (development [<20 years], n = 644, 1021 MRIs, follow-up interval = 1.7 years [1.0–3.2]; adulthood/aging [≥20 years], n = 330, 612 MRIs, follow-up interval = 1.6 years [0.2–6.6]), see Fjell et al., 2015 for details (sample descriptives are provided in Table 1).
evidence: This is a descriptive statistic of the dataset.

claim: Annual symmetrized percent change (APC) was calculated for each participant for each brain region using the formula APC = (Vol Tp2 – Vol Tp1) / (Vol Tp2 + Vol Tp1) × 100.
source: Annual symmetrized percent change (APC) was calculated for each participant for each brain region, averaged over hemispheres, using the formula APC = (Vol Tp2 – Vol Tp1) / (Vol Tp2 + Vol Tp1) × 100.
evidence: This describes the method used to calculate change.

claim: The Louvain algorithm for detecting communities in networks was applied to derive clusters in the correlation matrix from the development sample.
source: The Louvain algorithm for detecting communities in networks (Blondel et al., 2008a) was applied to derive clusters in the correlation matrix from the development sample, and the Mantel test run to compare the different matrices.
evidence: This describes the analytical method used.

claim: Five clusters of coordinated developmental change were identified.
source: Five clusters of coordinated developmental change were identified (Figure 1) (see Cluster stability analyses and Validation analyses below for a more detailed discussion and justification of the cluster solution).
evidence: This is a main finding of the study.

claim: The community-structure solution was significantly more clustered than in random networks (p<0.001).
source: The community-structure solution was significantly more clustered than in the random networks (p<0.001, developmental change Q=0.44, the 2.5 and 97.5 percentile of the random Q distribution=0.36–0.40).
evidence: This is a statistical finding supporting the validity of the cluster solution.

claim: The developmental change Q value was 0.44.
source: The community-structure solution was significantly more clustered than in the random networks (p<0.001, developmental change Q=0.44, the 2.5 and 97.5 percentile of the random Q distribution=0.36–0.40).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the analysis.

claim: Cluster 1 consisted of the ventricles.
source: Three large clusters consisted of the ventricles (Cluster 1); the brain stem, cerebellum white matter (WM) and cerebellum cortex, cortical WM, thalamus and hippocampus (Cluster 2); and cortex, putamen, amygdala, and nucleus accumbens (Cluster 3).
evidence: This describes the composition of one of the identified clusters.

claim: Cluster 2 consisted of the brain stem, cerebellum white matter (WM) and cerebellum cortex, cortical WM, thalamus and hippocampus.
source: Three large clusters consisted of the ventricles (Cluster 1); the brain stem, cerebellum white matter (WM) and cerebellum cortex, cortical WM, thalamus and hippocampus (Cluster 2); and cortex, putamen, amygdala, and nucleus accumbens (Cluster 3).
evidence: This describes the composition of one of the identified clusters.

claim: Cluster 3 consisted of cortex, putamen, amygdala, and nucleus accumbens.
source: Three large clusters consisted of the ventricles (Cluster 1); the brain stem, cerebellum white matter (WM) and cerebellum cortex, cortical WM, thalamus and hippocampus (Cluster 2); and cortex, putamen, amygdala, and nucleus accumbens (Cluster 3).
evidence: This describes the composition of one of the identified clusters.

claim: Caudate was represented by a separate cluster (Cluster 4).
source: Caudate (Cluster 4) and pallidum (Cluster 5) were represented by separate clusters.
evidence: This describes the composition of one of the identified clusters.

claim: Pallidum was represented by a separate cluster (Cluster 5).
source: Caudate (Cluster 4) and pallidum (Cluster 5) were represented by separate clusters.
evidence: This describes the composition of one of the identified clusters.

claim: The change–change matrices from development and adult/aging were more similar than expected by chance (r = 0.72, p<0.0001).
source: To this end, the pairwise change–change correlations between regions were calculated for the adult and aging sample (Figure 2), and the Mantel test was run to compare the developmental and the adult/aging matrices. The change–change matrices were more similar than expected by chance, r = 0.72 (p<0.0001), demonstrating substantial overlap of clusters of change in development and aging.
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the Mantel test.

claim: There is substantial overlap of clusters of change in development and aging.
source: The change–change matrices were more similar than expected by chance, r = 0.72 (p<0.0001), demonstrating substantial overlap of clusters of change in development and aging.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the statistical finding.

claim: The results were replicated using longitudinal data from the Lifebrain consortium (r = 0.71, p<0.0001).
source: The results were replicated using longitudinal data from the Lifebrain consortium (total n = 756, 1512 MRIs, mean follow-up interval = 2.3 years, age 19–89 years, mean 59.8 years), yielding almost identical results (r = 0.71, p<0.0001).
evidence: This describes a replication of the main finding in an independent dataset.

claim: The Lifebrain consortium dataset included 756 participants with 1512 MRIs, mean follow-up interval = 2.3 years, age 19–89 years, mean 59.8 years.
source: The results were replicated using longitudinal data from the Lifebrain consortium (total n = 756, 1512 MRIs, mean follow-up interval = 2.3 years, age 19–89 years, mean 59.8 years), yielding almost identical results (r = 0.71, p<0.0001).
evidence: This describes the replication dataset.

claim: Consensus clustering combined with the versatility metric was used to assess the stability of the identified clusters.
source: As a sensitivity analysis, we performed consensus clustering (Lancichinetti and Fortunato, 2012; Romero-Garcia et al., 2018) combined with the versatility metric to aid selection of the resolution parameter γ for the Louvain algorithm (Shinn et al., 2017).
evidence: This describes a sensitivity analysis method.

claim: Using the default resolution parameter γ = 1 for consensus clustering yielded an identical solution to the main analysis.
source: In the main analysis, we used the default resolution parameter γ = 1, and using this for the consensus clustering yielded an identical solution.
evidence: This is a finding from the sensitivity analysis.

claim: The five-cluster solution was the most frequent and showed the lowest versatility over several γ levels.
source: Thus, the five-cluster solution was the most frequent and showed the lowest versatility over several γ levels.
evidence: This is a finding from the sensitivity analysis supporting the main cluster solution.

claim: The five-cluster solution appeared seven times compared with once for the three- and eight-cluster solutions and twice for the six- and seven-cluster solutions.
source: Specifically, the five-cluster solution appeared seven times compared with once for the three- and eight-cluster solutions and twice for the six- and seven-cluster solutions.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the sensitivity analysis.

claim: The developmental and the adult/aging change–change matrices were more similar than expected by chance based on normalized mutual information (NMI = 0.65, p=0.003).
source: All of these metrics supported the conclusion that the developmental and the adulthood/ aging change matrices were more similar than expected by chance (NMI = 0.65, p=0.003; VI = 0.96, p=0.0002; zRand = 5.33, p<0.0001).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the validation analysis.

claim: The developmental and the adult/aging change–change matrices were more similar than expected by chance based on variation of information (VI = 0.96, p=0.0002).
source: All of these metrics supported the conclusion that the developmental and the adulthood/ aging change matrices were more similar than expected by chance (NMI = 0.65, p=0.003; VI = 0.96, p=0.0002; zRand = 5.33, p<0.0001).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the validation analysis.

claim: The developmental and the adult/aging change–change matrices were more similar than expected by chance based on the z-score of the Rand coefficient (zRand = 5.33, p<0.0001).
source: All of these metrics supported the conclusion that the developmental and the adulthood/ aging change matrices were more similar than expected by chance (NMI = 0.65, p=0.003; VI = 0.96, p=0.0002; zRand = 5.33, p<0.0001).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the validation analysis.

claim: Pairwise genetic correlations of the slope factor (change) between all regions were computed using multivariate latent change score models in the VETSA sample.
source: Using multivariate latent change score models, we calculated the differences in subcortical volumes from baseline to follow-up in the Vietnam Era Twin Study of Aging (n = 331, mean follow-up interval = 5.5 years) and computed pairwise genetic correlations of the slope factor (i.e., change) between all regions (see Brouwer et al., 2017 for details on the statistical twin model).
evidence: This describes the method used for genetic analysis.

claim: The VETSA sample included 331 participants with a mean follow-up interval of 5.5 years.
source: Using multivariate latent change score models, we calculated the differences in subcortical volumes from baseline to follow-up in the Vietnam Era Twin Study of Aging (n = 331, mean follow-up interval = 5.5 years) and computed pairwise genetic correlations of the slope factor (i.e., change) between all regions (see Brouwer et al., 2017 for details on the statistical twin model).
evidence: This describes the dataset used for genetic analysis.

claim: The matrix of shared genetic influences on change between each pair of brain structures was statistically more similar to the pattern of correlated changes during development (r = 0.46, p=9.999e−05).
source: The Mantel test confirmed that the shared genetic influences on the change–change relationships were statistically more similar to the pattern of correlated changes during development (r = 0.46, p=9.999e−05) and aging (r = 0.37, p<0.0002) than expected by chance.
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the genetic analysis.

claim: The matrix of shared genetic influences on change between each pair of brain structures was statistically more similar to the pattern of correlated changes during aging (r = 0.37, p<0.0002).
source: The Mantel test confirmed that the shared genetic influences on the change–change relationships were statistically more similar to the pattern of correlated changes during development (r = 0.46, p=9.999e−05) and aging (r = 0.37, p<0.0002) than expected by chance.
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the genetic analysis.

claim: Replication using Lifebrain data yielded r = 0.37 (p<0.0004) between the matrix of shared genetic influences on change and the Lifebrain aging change–change correlation matrix.
source: Replication was again run using Lifebrain data, yielding r = 0.37 (p<0.0004) between the matrix of shared genetic influences on change and the Lifebrain aging change–change correlation matrix.
evidence: This is a replication finding from the genetic analysis.

claim: Statistical power was too low to yield valid estimates of pairwise SNP-based genetic correlation between change in each pair of structures using 1337 participants with longitudinal MRIs from UK Biobank and 508 from LCBC.
source: In order to further explore the genetic contributions to coordinated subcortical change, we first attempted to calculate the pairwise single-nucleotide polymorphism (SNP)-based genetic correlation between change in each pair of structures by running a mega-analysis on 1337 participants with longitudinal MRIs from UK Biobank and 508 from LCBC. However, this initial analysis showed that statistical power – as could be expected – was too low to yield valid estimates.
evidence: This describes a limitation encountered in the analysis.

claim: The SNP genetic correlation matrix was more similar to the developmental change matrix than expected by chance (r = 0.57, p<0.0005).
source: The Mantel test (r = 0.57, p<0.0005) demonstrated that the SNP genetic correlation matrix was more similar to the developmental change matrix than expected by chance.
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the SNP genetic analysis.

claim: The genetic organization of subcortical structures in middle-age can be predicted from the organization of change during brain development in childhood.
source: This showed that the genetic organization of subcortical structures in middle-age can be predicted from the organization of change during brain development in childhood.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the SNP genetic analysis finding.

claim: The SNP genetic correlation matrix was more similar to the aging change matrix than expected by chance (r = 0.56, p<0.0003).
source: For completeness, we also compared the SNP genetic correlation matrix to the aging change matrix (r = 0.56, p<0.0003) and the heritability of coordinated change matrix from the VETSA sample (r = 0.38, p<0.0003), in both cases showing significantly higher similarity than expected by chance.
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the SNP genetic analysis.

claim: The SNP genetic correlation matrix was more similar to the heritability of coordinated change matrix from the VETSA sample than expected by chance (r = 0.38, p<0.0003).
source: For completeness, we also compared the SNP genetic correlation matrix to the aging change matrix (r = 0.56, p<0.0003) and the heritability of coordinated change matrix from the VETSA sample (r = 0.38, p<0.0003), in both cases showing significantly higher similarity than expected by chance.
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the SNP genetic analysis.

claim: The UKB SNP genetic correlation matrix showed excellent coherence with the Lifebrain replication sample (r = 0.47, p<0.0006).
source: The UKB SNP genetic correlation matrix also showed excellent coherence with the Lifebrain replication sample (r = 0.47, p<0.0006) and with the change–change matrix derived from the 1337 UKB participants with longitudinal MRI (r = 0.46, p<0.0002).
evidence: This is a statistical finding showing replication.

claim: The UKB SNP genetic correlation matrix showed excellent coherence with the change–change matrix derived from the 1337 UKB participants with longitudinal MRI (r = 0.46, p<0.0002).
source: The UKB SNP genetic correlation matrix also showed excellent coherence with the Lifebrain replication sample (r = 0.47, p<0.0006) and with the change–change matrix derived from the 1337 UKB participants with longitudinal MRI (r = 0.46, p<0.0002).
evidence: This is a statistical finding showing replication.

claim: The regions of Cluster 2 mainly emerged from rhombencephalon or the posterior prosencephalon.
source: The regions of Cluster 2 mainly emerged from rhombencephalon or the posterior prosencephalon, making up structures placed low on the cranial vertical axis, including brain stem (myelencephalon), cerebellum cortex and WM (metencephalon), and the thalamus (diencephalon).
evidence: This describes the embryonic origins of structures in Cluster 2.

claim: Cluster 2 structures are placed low on the cranial vertical axis.
source: The regions of Cluster 2 mainly emerged from rhombencephalon or the posterior prosencephalon, making up structures placed low on the cranial vertical axis, including brain stem (myelencephalon), cerebellum cortex and WM (metencephalon), and the thalamus (diencephalon).
evidence: This describes the placement of Cluster 2 structures along the cranial axis.

claim: The hippocampus and the cortical WM were also included in Cluster 2, which is an exception to the embryonic developmental principle.
source: The exception to this was that the hippocampus and the cortical WM were also included in Cluster 2.
evidence: This notes an exception to the general pattern observed.

claim: The extensive connectivity between cerebellum and cerebrum may explain the inclusion of cortical WM in Cluster 2.
source: The extensive connectivity between cerebellum and cerebrum, and the similarities in development of WM in cerebellum and cerebrum, may explain the latter finding.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for an observed pattern.

claim: The similarities in development of WM in cerebellum and cerebrum may explain the inclusion of cortical WM in Cluster 2.
source: The extensive connectivity between cerebellum and cerebrum, and the similarities in development of WM in cerebellum and cerebrum, may explain the latter finding.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for an observed pattern.

claim: Clusters 3–5 comprised structures developed from subpallium/ventral telencephalon (caudate, pallidum, putamen) and pallium/dorsal encephalon (amygdala, cortex).
source: Clusters 3–5 comprised structures developed from subpallium/ventral telencephalon (caudate, pallidum, putamen) and pallium/dorsal encephalon (amygdala, cortex), also showing consistency with the major principles from embryonic development and placement along the cranial vertical axis.
evidence: This describes the embryonic origins of structures in Clusters 3-5.

claim: Clusters 3–5 show consistency with the major principles from embryonic development and placement along the cranial vertical axis.
source: Clusters 3–5 comprised structures developed from subpallium/ventral telencephalon (caudate, pallidum, putamen) and pallium/dorsal encephalon (amygdala, cortex), also showing consistency with the major principles from embryonic development and placement along the cranial vertical axis.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the clustering results in relation to embryonic development.

claim: Each cluster and regional volume was expected to yield unique age trajectories during development and adulthood.
source: Each cluster and regional volume was expected to yield unique age trajectories during development and adulthood.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the clustering results.

claim: Cluster 1 increased linearly during development, although the rate of increase was modest.
source: Cluster 1 increased linearly, although the rate of increase was modest.
evidence: This describes the developmental trajectory of Cluster 1.

claim: Cluster 2 showed a decreasing exponential function with volume increase leveling off after 15 years.
source: Cluster 2 showed a decreasing exponential function with volume increase leveling off after 15 years.
evidence: This describes the developmental trajectory of Cluster 2.

claim: Cluster 3 mimicked a cubic relationship, with a slight increase in volume until about 8 years, then steeper reductions, which were gradually smaller from 15 years.
source: Cluster 3 mimicked a cubic relationship, with a slight increase in volume until about 8 years, then steeper reductions, which were gradually smaller from 15 years.
evidence: This describes the developmental trajectory of Cluster 3.

claim: Cluster 4 (caudate) showed an inverted U-shaped trajectory with a sharp increase until about 9 years.
source: Cluster 4 (caudate) showed an inverted U-shaped trajectory with a sharp increase until about 9 years, and Cluster 5 (pallidum) showed a cubic trajectory with similarities to Cluster 3.
evidence: This describes the developmental trajectory of Cluster 4.

claim: Cluster 5 (pallidum) showed a cubic trajectory with similarities to Cluster 3.
source: Cluster 4 (caudate) showed an inverted U-shaped trajectory with a sharp increase until about 9 years, and Cluster 5 (pallidum) showed a cubic trajectory with similarities to Cluster 3.
evidence: This describes the developmental trajectory of Cluster 5.

claim: The trajectories across the adult age-range differed qualitatively between clusters in terms of steepness and shape.
source: The trajectories across the adult age-range differed qualitatively between clusters in terms of steepness and shape.
evidence: This describes differences in aging trajectories between clusters.

claim: The trajectory for each cluster represented a continuation of the developmental trend seen in childhood and adolescence.
source: The trajectory for each cluster represented a continuation of the developmental trend seen in childhood and adolescence.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the trajectory findings showing lifespan continuity.

claim: Cluster 1 showed an exponential increase in adulthood and aging.
source: Cluster 1 showed an exponential increase, Cluster 2 an inverted U-shaped trajectory, Clusters 3 and 4 almost linear reductions, while Cluster 5 showed reductions until about 50 years and little or no change after that.
evidence: This describes the aging trajectory of Cluster 1.

claim: Cluster 2 showed an inverted U-shaped trajectory in adulthood and aging.
source: Cluster 1 showed an exponential increase, Cluster 2 an inverted U-shaped trajectory, Clusters 3 and 4 almost linear reductions, while Cluster 5 showed reductions until about 50 years and little or no change after that.
evidence: This describes the aging trajectory of Cluster 2.

claim: Clusters 3 and 4 showed almost linear reductions in adulthood and aging.
source: Cluster 1 showed an exponential increase, Cluster 2 an inverted U-shaped trajectory, Clusters 3 and 4 almost linear reductions, while Cluster 5 showed reductions until about 50 years and little or no change after that.
evidence: This describes the aging trajectories of Clusters 3 and 4.

claim: Cluster 5 showed reductions until about 50 years and little or no change after that in adulthood and aging.
source: Cluster 1 showed an exponential increase, Cluster 2 an inverted U-shaped trajectory, Clusters 3 and 4 almost linear reductions, while Cluster 5 showed reductions until about 50 years and little or no change after that.
evidence: This describes the aging trajectory of Cluster 5.

claim: Cluster 1 showed a significant relationship to general cognitive function (GCA) (t = 3.74, p=0.00018).
source: Corrected for five comparisons, two clusters showed significant (p<0.01) relationships to GCA, that is Cluster 1 (t = 3.74, p=0.00018) and Cluster 3 (t = 2.75, p=0.006).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the cognitive analysis.

claim: Cluster 3 showed a significant relationship to general cognitive function (GCA) (t = 2.75, p=0.006).
source: Corrected for five comparisons, two clusters showed significant (p<0.01) relationships to GCA, that is Cluster 1 (t = 3.74, p=0.00018) and Cluster 3 (t = 2.75, p=0.006).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the cognitive analysis.

claim: Low GCA score was associated with lower volumes in Clusters 1 and 3.
source: Low GCA score was associated with lower volumes.
evidence: This describes the direction of the relationship between cognition and volume.

claim: For Cluster 1, a significant interaction between GCA and age was found (F = 4.59, p=0.01).
source: For Cluster 1 was a significant interaction between GCA and age found (F = 4.59, p=0.01), while for Cluster 3, age trajectories did not differ significantly as a function of GCA (all p's>0.46), thus showing stable relationships across life.
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the cognitive analysis.

claim: For Cluster 3, age trajectories did not differ significantly as a function of GCA (all p's>0.46), showing stable relationships across life.
source: For Cluster 1 was a significant interaction between GCA and age found (F = 4.59, p=0.01), while for Cluster 3, age trajectories did not differ significantly as a function of GCA (all p's>0.46), thus showing stable relationships across life.
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the cognitive analysis.

claim: The intra-cluster correlations were significantly higher than the extra-cluster correlations in all the tested samples, except for Cluster 3 in the VETSA sample.
source: The intra-cluster correlations were significantly higher than the extra-cluster correlations in all the tested samples, except for Cluster 3 in the VETSA sample (Table 5).
evidence: This is a validation finding supporting the cluster solution.

claim: When excluding the ventricles, the coherence between matrices was reduced but was still significant for all comparisons except UKB.
source: As expected, the coherence between matrices was reduced, but was still significant for all comparisons, except UKB (Dev vs LCBC adulthood and aging r = 0.44, p<0.009; Lifebrain r = 0.41, p<0.0008; VETSA r = 0.44, p<0.0009; UKB r = −0.06, p=0.63).
evidence: This is a sensitivity analysis finding.

claim: The Mantel test comparing patterns of developmental to adult and aging changes in 12 genetically defined cortical regions yielded a correlation of r = 0.83.
source: Finally, we ran the Mantel test comparing the patterns of developmental to adult and aging changes in 12 genetically defined cortical regions from the same LCBC participants (see Chen et al., 2013; Fjell et al., 2015). This yielded a correlation of r = 0.83, which suggests that the organization of developmental subcortical change is conserved through life, but to a somewhat lesser extent than the organization of cortical change.
evidence: This is a comparative finding between cortical and subcortical regions.

claim: The organization of developmental subcortical change is conserved through life, but to a somewhat lesser extent than the organization of cortical change.
source: This yielded a correlation of r = 0.83, which suggests that the organization of developmental subcortical change is conserved through life, but to a somewhat lesser extent than the organization of cortical change.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the comparative finding.

claim: Volumetric change of subcortical structures in development forms meaningful clusters.
source: The results demonstrate that volumetric change of subcortical structures in development forms meaningful clusters.
evidence: This is a main conclusion of the study.

claim: The clusters tend to follow the main cranial vertical axis from embryonic brain development, suggesting continuity from earlier to later stages of development.
source: These clusters tend to follow the main cranial vertical axis from embryonic brain development, suggesting continuity from earlier to later stages of development.
evidence: This is a main conclusion of the study.

claim: The lifespan trajectories of subcortical structures are more divergent than those for cortical regions.
source: Although the lifespan trajectories of subcortical structures are more divergent than those for cortical regions (Fjell et al., 2014; Walhovd et al., 2011), the clusters were conserved through life.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The clusters were conserved through life despite more divergent trajectories of subcortical structures.
source: Although the lifespan trajectories of subcortical structures are more divergent than those for cortical regions (Fjell et al., 2014; Walhovd et al., 2011), the clusters were conserved through life.
evidence: This is a main finding of the study.

claim: Regional subcortical volumetric changes in aging follow a similar pattern as developmental changes in childhood.
source: Thus, similar to what has been shown for the cerebral cortex (Fjell et al., 2015), regional subcortical volumetric changes in aging follow a similar pattern as developmental changes in childhood.
evidence: This is a main conclusion of the study.

claim: The findings make a strong case for the theory that early life sets the stage for aging.
source: This makes a strong case for the theory that early life sets the stage for aging (Jagust, 2016; Walhovd et al., 2016a; Yeatman et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings in the context of existing theory.

claim: The volumetric correlations within each cluster and the coordinated volumetric change of each cluster tended to be governed by common sets of genes.
source: Importantly, the volumetric correlations within each cluster and the coordinated volumetric change of each cluster tended to be governed by common sets of genes.
evidence: This is a main conclusion of the study.

claim: Coordination of volumetric change across subcortical structures adheres to similar principles of lifespan continuity and genetic organization previously seen for the cortex.
source: Thus, coordination of volumetric change across subcortical structures adheres to similar principles of lifespan continuity and genetic organization previously seen for the cortex.
evidence: This is a main conclusion of the study.

claim: The findings support the hypothesis that genetically governed neurodevelopmental processes can be traced in subcortical structures throughout life.
source: This supports the hypothesis that genetically governed neurodevelopmental processes can be traced in subcortical structures throughout life.
evidence: This is a main conclusion of the study.

claim: The topographical development of cortical thickness is well described, with regional variability that follows certain functional, anatomical, and genetic principles of organization.
source: The topographical development of cortical thickness is well described, with regional variability that follows certain functional, anatomical, and genetic principles of organization (Chen et al., 2013; Fjell et al., 2019; Fjell et al., 2015; Raznahan et al., 2011; Tamnes et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Compared to the cerebral cortex, subcortical structures show highly divergent lifespan trajectories.
source: Compared to the cerebral cortex, subcortical structures show highly divergent lifespan trajectories (Fjell et al., 2013; Ostby et al., 2009; Raznahan et al., 2014) and follow fundamentally different ontogenetic and phylogenetic principles (Tuller et al., 2008; Zhang and Li, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Meaningful clusters of developmental volumetric change were identified.
source: Meaningful clusters of developmental volumetric change were identified, with divergent developmental trajectories.
evidence: This is a main finding of the study.

claim: The different regions tended to cluster according to their embryonic origins.
source: Importantly, the different regions tended to cluster according to their embryonic origins.
evidence: This is a main finding of the study.

claim: Hippocampus is part of the cerebral cortex, but develops from the medial pallium in contrast to the neocortex.
source: Hippocampus is part of the cerebral cortex, but develops from the medial pallium in contrast to the neocortex.
evidence: This is anatomical and developmental knowledge.

claim: Compared to many regions in the cerebral cortex, hippocampus has a more similar appearance across the range of mammal species.
source: Compared to many regions in the cerebral cortex, hippocampus has a more similar appearance across the range of mammal species (Bingman and Salas, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Cortical WM originates from the anterior prosencephalon, but the major part of myelination occurs postnatally.
source: Cortical WM originates from the anterior prosencephalon, but the major part of myelination occurs postnatally, so this compartment of the brain is not easily placed within the same embryonic developmental context.
evidence: This is developmental knowledge.

claim: The WM label is anatomically gross with substantial regional differences in development.
source: In addition, the WM label is anatomically gross with substantial regional differences in development (Tamnes et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Cluster 2 is characterized by relatively high myelin content among several of its constituents.
source: This cluster is also characterized by relatively high myelin content among several of its constituents, which may have contributed to the inclusion of hippocampus and cortical WM.
evidence: This is an observation about the cluster composition.

claim: At a general level, change in the structures tended to cluster according to trends from embryonic development and placement along the cranial vertical axis.
source: Nevertheless, at a general level, change in the structures tended to cluster according to trends from embryonic development and placement along the cranial vertical axis.
evidence: This is a main conclusion of the study.

claim: The coherence between the developmental clusters and embryonic brain development is based on a qualitative judgment.
source: It must be noted as a limitation that the coherence between the developmental clusters and embryonic brain development is based on a qualitative judgment.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a limitation in the analysis.

claim: Subcortical structures that developed together during childhood tended to change together in adulthood and aging.
source: We found that subcortical structures that developed together during childhood tended to change together in adulthood and aging.
evidence: This is a main finding of the study.

claim: Longitudinal volumetric change in regions that cluster together tend to show overlapping genetic influences.
source: We found that longitudinal volumetric change in regions that cluster together tend to show overlapping genetic influences.
evidence: This is a main finding of the study.

claim: Regions that develop and change together through life to a certain degree are influenced by shared sets of genes.
source: This suggests that regions that develop and change together through life to a certain degree are influenced by shared sets of genes.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the genetic findings.

claim: The SNP analysis showed that the cross-sectional volumetric relationships followed a similar organization to the longitudinal change patterns.
source: Furthermore, the SNP analysis showed that also the cross-sectional volumetric relationships followed a similar organization.
evidence: This is a finding from the SNP genetic analysis.

claim: There is a genetic basis for the consistent pattern of change in subcortical structures from development through the rest of life.
source: Thus, there seems to be a genetic basis for the consistent pattern of change in subcortical structures from development through the rest of life.
evidence: This is a main conclusion of the study.

claim: Significant heritability estimates for brain changes have been demonstrated in ENIGMA.
source: It must be noted that although significant heritability estimates for brain changes have been demonstrated in ENIGMA, evidence for genetic variants specific for brain change was found for cerebellar GM and the lateral ventricles only (Brouwer et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Evidence for genetic variants specific for brain change was found for cerebellar GM and the lateral ventricles only in ENIGMA.
source: It must be noted that although significant heritability estimates for brain changes have been demonstrated in ENIGMA, evidence for genetic variants specific for brain change was found for cerebellar GM and the lateral ventricles only (Brouwer et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Genetic influence on volumetric change rates and baseline volume tended to overlap for most structures.
source: Although limited statistical power prevented strong conclusions, genetic influence on volumetric change rates and baseline volume tended to overlap for most structures.
evidence: This is a finding from the genetic analysis with a caveat about statistical power.

claim: Regions within each developmental cluster tended to show overlapping genetic influences based on SNP analyses.
source: Using the expanded sample for the SNP analyses, we found further evidence that regions within each developmental cluster tended to show overlapping genetic influences.
evidence: This is a finding from the SNP genetic analysis.

claim: A previous multi-sample GWAS reported significant genetic correlations between some of the subcortical structures tested in the present study.
source: A previous multi-sample GWAS also reported significant genetic correlations between some of the subcortical structures tested in the present study (Satizabal et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The similarity of the developmental volumetric change–change matrix and the SNP genetic volume–volume correlation matrix from middle-aged adults yielded further support for the hypothesis that genetically governed neurodevelopmental processes can be traced through life.
source: The similarity of the developmental volumetric change–change matrix and the SNP genetic volume–volume correlation matrix from middle-aged adults thus yielded further support for the hypothesis that genetically governed neurodevelopmental processes can be traced through life.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the genetic findings.

claim: The results revealed close correspondence between the genetic organization of subcortical structures and their embryonic origins.
source: Moreover, the results revealed close correspondence between the genetic organization of subcortical structures and their embryonic origins, which suggest a link from embryonic brain development to the brain's genetic architecture in adulthood and aging.
evidence: This is a main conclusion of the study.

claim: There is a link from embryonic brain development to the brain's genetic architecture in adulthood and aging.
source: Moreover, the results revealed close correspondence between the genetic organization of subcortical structures and their embryonic origins, which suggest a link from embryonic brain development to the brain's genetic architecture in adulthood and aging.
evidence: This is a main conclusion of the study.

claim: High genetic correlations were identified between hippocampus and amygdala.
source: It must also be mentioned that high genetic correlations were identified between some structures from different clusters. This was especially true for hippocampus and amygdala, which showed high genetic change–change correlations in VETSA and genetic cross-sectional correlations in UKB.
evidence: This is a finding from the genetic analysis.

claim: Hippocampus and amygdala showed high genetic change–change correlations in VETSA and genetic cross-sectional correlations in UKB.
source: This was especially true for hippocampus and amygdala, which showed high genetic change–change correlations in VETSA and genetic cross-sectional correlations in UKB.
evidence: This is a finding from the genetic analysis.

claim: This study provides approximations of the underlying neurobiology, similar to all studies based on in vivo imaging methods.
source: Similar to all studies based on in vivo imaging methods, this study provides approximations of the underlying neurobiology.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a general limitation of MRI studies.

claim: The MRI-derived measures are estimations, and the segmentations are based on signal intensities and contrast properties that are prone to the influence of multiple factors.
source: The MRI-derived measures are estimations, and the segmentations are based on signal intensities and contrast properties that are prone to the influence of multiple factors (Walhovd et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a limitation supported by a citation.

claim: Underlying mechanisms of volume differences and change are complex and may involve events such as aborization of axons and dendrites, axonal sprouting and loss, dendritic degeneration, vascular elaboration, synaptic pruning, as well as growth and reductions of myelination.
source: Underlying mechanisms of volume differences and change are complex and may involve events such as aborization of axons and dendrites, axonal sprouting and loss, dendritic degeneration, vascular elaboration, synaptic pruning, as well as growth and reductions of myelination (see Fjell and Walhovd, 2010 for a discussion of these issues).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous discussion of these issues.

claim: Age differences in cortical GM–WM contrast have been previously shown.
source: We have previously shown age differences in cortical GM–WM contrast (Westlye et al., 2009) and T1w signal intensities (Westlye et al., 2010), which can also be detected longitudinally (Vidal-Piñeiro et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Age differences in T1w signal intensities have been previously shown.
source: We have previously shown age differences in cortical GM–WM contrast (Westlye et al., 2009) and T1w signal intensities (Westlye et al., 2010), which can also be detected longitudinally (Vidal-Piñeiro et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Age-related changes in GM-WM contrast and T1w signal intensities can be detected longitudinally.
source: We have previously shown age differences in cortical GM–WM contrast (Westlye et al., 2009) and T1w signal intensities (Westlye et al., 2010), which can also be detected longitudinally (Vidal-Piñeiro et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The present results reflect effects of various neurobiological events on signal intensities and contrast.
source: The present results thus reflect effects of various neurobiological events on signal intensities and contrast.
evidence: This is an interpretation of what the MRI measures represent.

claim: Myelin content has a major impact on T1w intensities.
source: For instance, as mentioned above, myelin content has a major impact on T1w intensities, and myelin content is strongly related to age in development and aging (Grydeland et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Myelin content is strongly related to age in development and aging.
source: For instance, as mentioned above, myelin content has a major impact on T1w intensities, and myelin content is strongly related to age in development and aging (Grydeland et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The clustering results will likely partly reflect different myelin content in the structures analyzed.
source: Thus, the clustering results will likely partly reflect different myelin content in the structures analyzed, as changes in myelin may be correlated across regions in the brain.
evidence: This is a speculation about what contributes to the clustering results.

claim: Changes in myelin may be correlated across regions in the brain.
source: Thus, the clustering results will likely partly reflect different myelin content in the structures analyzed, as changes in myelin may be correlated across regions in the brain.
evidence: This is a speculation about myelin changes.

claim: A promising avenue for further research is to use multi-modal neuroimaging with different MRI sequences and analysis methods to yield more insight in the foundations for the volumetric changes.
source: A promising avenue for further research is to use multi-modal neuroimaging with different MRI sequences and analysis methods to yield more insight in the foundations for the volumetric changes.
evidence: This is a suggestion for future research.

claim: Although the clustering of regions is based on pairwise change–change correlations, this does not imply that each cluster consists of homogenous regions.
source: A second caveat is that although the clustering of regions is based on pairwise change–change correlations, this does not imply that each cluster consists of homogenous regions.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a limitation in interpreting the clusters.

claim: Regions within a cluster showed more correlated volumetric change and higher genetic correlations with other regions within the cluster than with regions outside the cluster.
source: Still, regions within a cluster showed more correlated volumetric change and higher genetic correlations with other regions within the cluster than with regions outside the cluster.
evidence: This is a finding that supports the validity of the clusters.

claim: Subcortical childhood development can be described according to meaningful clusters.
source: Subcortical childhood development can be described according to meaningful clusters, which are stable through life, tend to follow gradients of embryonic brain development, and tend to be influenced by shared sets of genes.
evidence: This is a main conclusion of the study.

claim: The developmental clusters are stable through life.
source: Subcortical childhood development can be described according to meaningful clusters, which are stable through life, tend to follow gradients of embryonic brain development, and tend to be influenced by shared sets of genes.
evidence: This is a main conclusion of the study.

claim: The developmental clusters tend to follow gradients of embryonic brain development.
source: Subcortical childhood development can be described according to meaningful clusters, which are stable through life, tend to follow gradients of embryonic brain development, and tend to be influenced by shared sets of genes.
evidence: This is a main conclusion of the study.

claim: The developmental clusters tend to be influenced by shared sets of genes.
source: Subcortical childhood development can be described according to meaningful clusters, which are stable through life, tend to follow gradients of embryonic brain development, and tend to be influenced by shared sets of genes.
evidence: This is a main conclusion of the study.

claim: The pattern of change in subcortical regions may best be understood in a lifespan perspective.
source: Thus, the pattern of change in subcortical regions may best be understood in a lifespan perspective.
evidence: This is a main conclusion of the study.

claim: The LCBC sample included 974 healthy participants (508 females/466 males), 4.1–88.5 years of age.
source: A total of 1633 valid scans from 974 healthy participants (508 females/466 males), 4.1–88.5 years of age (mean visit age 25.8, SD 24.1), were drawn from studies coordinated by the Research Group for Lifespan Changes in Brain and Cognition (LCBC), Department of Psychology, University of Oslo, Norway (Fjell et al., 2015).
evidence: This describes the LCBC sample.

claim: For 635 LCBC participants, one follow-up scan was available, while 24 of these had two follow-ups.
source: For 635 participants, one follow-up scan was available, while 24 of these had two follow-ups.
evidence: This describes the longitudinal structure of the LCBC sample.

claim: Mean follow-up interval in the LCBC sample was 2.30 years (0.15–6.63 years, SD 1.19).
source: Mean follow-up interval was 2.30 years (0.15–6.63 years, SD 1.19).
evidence: This is a descriptive statistic of the LCBC sample.

claim: Sample density was higher in childhood/adolescence than adulthood in the LCBC sample.
source: Sample density was higher in childhood/ adolescence than adulthood, since we expected more rapid changes during that age period (1006 observations < 10 years, 378 observations ≥ 20 and < 60 years, and 249 observations 60–88.5 years).
evidence: This describes the sampling strategy.

claim: All LCBC participants' scans were examined by a neuroradiologist and deemed free of significant injuries or conditions.
source: All participants' scans were examined by a neuroradiologist and deemed free of significant injuries or conditions.
evidence: This describes the quality control procedure.

claim: The LCBC studies were approved by the Regional Committee for Medical and Health Research Ethics South, Norway.
source: The studies were approved by the Regional Committee for Medical and Health Research Ethics South, Norway (2010/2359; ​2010/3407; ​2009/200).
evidence: This describes the ethical approval.

claim: Written informed consent was obtained from all LCBC participants older than 12 years of age and from a parent/guardian of volunteers under 16 years of age.
source: Written informed consent was obtained from all participants older than 12 years of age and from a parent/guardian of volunteers under 16 years of age.
evidence: This describes the consent procedure.

claim: Oral informed consent was obtained from all LCBC participants under 12 years of age.
source: Oral informed consent was obtained from all participants under 12 years of age.
evidence: This describes the consent procedure.

claim: The VETSA sample included 331 male twins (150 MZ/106 DZ paired twins/75 unpaired) with imaging data at two time points.
source: Three hundred and thirty-one male twins (150 MZ/106 DZ paired twins/75 unpaired) were randomly recruited from the Vietnam Era Twin Registry and had imaging data at two time points.
evidence: This describes the VETSA sample.

claim: The VETSA study was approved by the Institutional Review Board at the University of California, San Diego.
source: The study was approved by the Institutional Review Board at the University of California, San Diego.
evidence: This describes the ethical approval.

claim: Average age at baseline in VETSA was 56.3 (2.6) years and follow-up interval 5.5 (0.5) years.
source: Average age at baseline was 56.3 (2.6) years and follow-up interval 5.5 (0.5) years (see Kremen et al., 2013; Kremen et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a descriptive statistic of the VETSA sample.

claim: The VETSA sample is representative of US men in their age range based on demographic and health characteristics.
source: Based on demographic and health characteristics, the sample is representative of US men in their age range (Kremen et al., 2013; Schoeneborn and Heyman, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The Lifebrain Consortium included 756 participants with longitudinal MRI (1672 scans, baseline age 19–89 [mean = 59.8, SD = 16.4], mean follow-up interval 2.3 years, range 0.3–4.9, SD = 1.2).
source: Seven hundred and fifty-six participants with longitudinal MRI were included from the European Lifebrain project (1672 scans, baseline age 19–89 [mean = 59.8, SD = 16.4], mean follow-up interval 2.3 years, range 0.3–4.9, SD = 1.2) (https://www.lifebrain.uio.no/) (Fjell et al., 2019), including major European brain studies: Berlin Study of Aging-II (BASE-II) (Bertram et al., 2014; Gerstorf et al., 2016), the BETULA project (Nyberg et al., 2020), the Cambridge Centre for Ageing and Neuroscience study (Cam-CAN) (Shafto et al., 2014), and University of Barcelona brain studies (Abellaneda-Pérez et al., 2019; Rajaram et al., 2016; Vidal-Piñeiro et al., 2014).
evidence: This describes the Lifebrain sample.

claim: The Lifebrain study was approved by the Regional Committee for Medical and Health Research Ethics South, Norway.
source: The study was approved by the Regional Committee for Medical and Health Research Ethics South, Norway (2017/653).
evidence: This describes the ethical approval.

claim: Lifebrain participants were screened to be cognitively healthy and in general not suffer from conditions known to affect brain function.
source: Participants were screened to be cognitively healthy and in general not suffer from conditions known to affect brain function, such as dementia, major stroke, multiple sclerosis, etc.
evidence: This describes the inclusion criteria.

claim: Thirty-eight thousand one hundred and twenty-seven participants with available MRIs and quality checked genetic information were included from UK Biobank (40–69 years).
source: Thirty-eight thousand one hundred and twenty-seven participants with available MRIs and quality checked (QC) genetic information were included in the final analyses from UKB (40–69 years), see https://biobank.ndph.ox.ac.uk/.
evidence: This describes the UKB sample.

claim: UK Biobank has approval from the North West Multi-centre Research Ethics Committee.
source: UKB has approval from the North West Multi-centre Research Ethics Committee (MREC).
evidence: This describes the ethical approval.

claim: Quality control of the UKB genotype data was performed at the participant level by removing participants failing genotyping QC (n = 550) or with abnormal heterozygosity values (n = 969).
source: We performed quality control of the genotype data at the participant level by removing participants failing genotyping QC (n = 550) or with abnormal heterozygosity values (n = 969).
evidence: This describes the quality control procedure.

claim: Related subjects were removed from the UKB sample by computing kinship coefficients using PLINK with the option --kinship 0.0625.
source: After excluding these subjects, we further remove related subjects by computing kinship coefficients using the program PLINK (Chang et al., 2015), with the option --kinship 0.0625.
evidence: This describes the quality control procedure.

claim: At variant level, SNPs having minor allele frequency less than 0.01 or Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium test p-value < 10−6 were removed from the UKB analysis.
source: At variant level, we removed SNPs having minor allele frequency less than 0.01 or Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium test p-value < 10−6.
evidence: This describes the quality control procedure.

claim: In total, 784,356 SNPs were used in the subsequent UKB analysis.
source: In total, 784,356 SNPs were used in the subsequent analysis.
evidence: This describes the data used in the analysis.

claim: The bivariate linear mixed model with genome-based restricted maximum likelihood methods implemented in GCTA was used to compute genetic correlations for the volume measures for each pair of the 16 brain subcortical structures in UKB.
source: We used the bivariate linear mixed model with genome-based restricted maximum likelihood methods implemented in the program GCTA (Yang et al., 2011) to compute genetic correlations for the volume measures for each pair of the 16 brain subcortical structures.
evidence: This describes the analytical method.

claim: GCA was assessed by WASI for LCBC participants aged 6.5–89 years of age.
source: GCA was assessed by WASI (Wechsler, 1999) for participants aged 6.5–89 years of age, while scores for corresponding subtests (Vocabulary, Similarities, Block design, and Matrices) from the Wechsler Preschool and Primary Scale of intelligence – III (WPPSI-III) (Wechsler, 2008) were used for the youngest participants (<6.5 years) (see Walhovd et al., 2016a).
evidence: This describes the cognitive assessment method.

claim: All LCBC participants scored within normal IQ range (82–145) or normal range of scaled scores (mean of subtests, s = 6.67–17.33).
source: All participants scored within normal IQ range (82–145) or normal range of scaled scores (mean of subtests, s = 6.67–17.33).
evidence: This describes the cognitive characteristics of the sample.

claim: LCBC imaging data were acquired using a 12-channel head coil on a 1.5-Tesla Siemens Avanto scanner at Oslo University Hospital Rikshospitalet and St. Olav's University Hospital in Trondheim.
source: Imaging data for the LCBC sample were acquired using a 12-channel head coil on a 1.5-Tesla Siemens Avanto scanner (Siemens Medical Solutions, Erlangen, Germany) at Oslo University Hospital Rikshospitalet and St. Olav's University Hospital in Trondheim (see Walhovd et al., 2016a).
evidence: This describes the MRI acquisition.

claim: For all samples, subcortical volumes were obtained by use of FreeSurfer.
source: For all samples, subcortical volumes were obtained by use of FreeSurfer (http://surfer.nmr.mgh.harvard.edu/) (Dale et al., 1999; Dale and Sereno, 1993; Fischl et al., 2002), processed with the longitudinal stream (Reuter et al., 2012).
evidence: This describes the image processing method.

claim: FreeSurfer processing used the longitudinal stream.
source: For all samples, subcortical volumes were obtained by use of FreeSurfer (http://surfer.nmr.mgh.harvard.edu/) (Dale et al., 1999; Dale and Sereno, 1993; Fischl et al., 2002), processed with the longitudinal stream (Reuter et al., 2012).
evidence: This describes the image processing method.

claim: All children MRIs were manually rated for movement on a 1–4 scale, and only scans with ratings 1 and 2 were included in the analyses.
source: All children MRIs were manually rated for movement on a 1–4 scale, and only scans with ratings 1 and 2 (no visible or only very minor possible signs of movement) were included in the analyses, reducing the risk of movement affecting the results.
evidence: This describes the quality control procedure.

claim: All reconstructed surfaces were inspected and discarded if they did not pass internal quality control, leading to the exclusion of 46 participants from MoBa-Neurocog and nine from ND.
source: Also, all reconstructed surfaces were inspected and discarded if they did not pass internal quality control. This led to the exclusion of 46 participants from MoBa-Neurocog and nine from ND, reducing the total LCBC sample to the reported 1633 scans.
evidence: This describes the quality control procedure.

claim: FreeSurfer 5.3 was used for the LCBC and VETSA analyses.
source: FreeSurfer 5.3 was used for the LCBC and VETSA analyses, while Lifebrain and UKB MRI data were processed with FreeSurfer 6.0.
evidence: This describes the software version used.

claim: Lifebrain and UKB MRI data were processed with FreeSurfer 6.0.
source: FreeSurfer 5.3 was used for the LCBC and VETSA analyses, while Lifebrain and UKB MRI data were processed with FreeSurfer 6.0.
evidence: This describes the software version used.

claim: Genetic change correlations were obtained by latent change score analyses on the VETSA one and VETSA two subcortical data.
source: Genetic change correlations were obtained by latent change score analyses on the VETSA one and VETSA two subcortical data (see Brouwer et al., 2017).
evidence: This describes the analytical method.

claim: All VETSA subcortical volumes were adjusted for site and ICV.
source: All subcortical volumes were adjusted for site and ICV.
evidence: This describes the data preprocessing.

claim: A genetic correlation matrix was generated by estimating genetic correlations of slope factors between all pairwise combinations of subcortical structures in bivariate latent change models in VETSA.
source: A genetic correlation matrix was generated by estimating genetic correlations of slope factors between all pairwise combinations of subcortical structures in bivariate latent change models.
evidence: This describes the analytical method.

claim: For the UKB SNP analyses, the volume measures of the 16 subcortical structures were corrected for ICV and normalized to have zero mean and one standard deviation.
source: For the UKB SNP analyses, the volume measures of the 16 subcortical structures were corrected for ICV and normalized to have zero mean and one standard deviation, separately, before estimating genetic correlations.
evidence: This describes the data preprocessing.

claim: GAMM implemented in R using the package 'mgcv' was used to derive age trajectories for all structures based on the 1633 LCBC MRIs.
source: GAMM implemented in R (http://www.r-project.org) using the package 'mgcv' (Wood, 2006) was used to derive age trajectories for all structures based on the 1633 LCBC MRIs.
evidence: This describes the analytical method.

claim: The Louvain algorithm is part of the Brain Connectivity Toolbox.
source: To identify clusters of correlations that could be compared across matrices, the community structure or modules in the matrices were obtained using the Louvain algorithm (Blondel et al., 2008b), part of the Brain Connectivity Toolbox (http://www.brain-connectivity-toolbox.net Rubinov and Sporns, 2010).
evidence: This describes the software used.

claim: 10,000 iterations of the Louvain algorithm were run, and each region assigned to the module it was most often associated with.
source: The community structure may vary from run to run due to heuristics in the algorithm pertaining to the order in which the nodes are considered, so 10,000 iterations of the algorithm were run, and each region assigned to the module it was most often associated with (by taking the mode of the module assignment across iterations).
evidence: This describes the analytical procedure.

claim: Negative values were treated asymmetrically in the clustering analysis.
source: Negative values were treated asymmetrically (Rubinov and Sporns, 2011).
evidence: This describes the analytical procedure.

claim: Between-regional correlations were de-meaned before they were entered into the clustering analyses to account for global brain changes.
source: To account for global brain changes, between-regional correlations were de-meaned before they were entered into the clustering analyses.
evidence: This describes the analytical procedure.
